title: Registered land: registration and priority
subtitle: Registrable dispositions, the priority rule, and what protects an interest against a buyer
objectives: Explain why certain dispositions of registered land must be completed by registration, and what happens before they are
State the basic priority rule in LRA 2002 and identify how an entry of notice changes the outcome for a later registered proprietor
Apply the alteration and indemnity provisions to a fact pattern where a mistake has been made on the register

leadingAuthorities.role: Defines registrable dispositions and sets the basic priority rule for registered land
The registration itself, not the underlying transaction, is what vests the legal estate
Governs alteration and rectification of the register
Governs indemnity for loss caused by rectification or by a mistake whose correction is refused

leadingAuthorities.citation: Swift 1st Ltd v Chief Land Registrar [2015] EWCA Civ 330
leadingAuthorities.role: Clarifies the boundary between alteration and rectification, and when indemnity is payable

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Registration questions reward students who treat the register as a machine with defined inputs and outputs, not as a story. Where the profile shows application is ahead of the underlying mechanics, this note appears: 'You're good at spotting the right answer — this lesson checks you know which provision actually produces it.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You know the sections. The test pool below leans on fact patterns — registration gaps, competing buyers, register mistakes — where you have to run the machine, not just name its parts.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Parts 1 and 2. Everything after that assumes you can say, without hesitating, what a registrable disposition is and why registration — not completion — is the moment that matters.

overview.hook: Think of the Land Register as a machine, not a filing cabinet. Feed it a disposition and it does three things at once: it mirrors the true state of title back at anyone who looks, it lets a buyer ignore whatever sits behind the curtain of ownership they can't see, and it insures against its own mistakes. This lesson is about how the machine actually runs — what goes in, what comes out, and who gets paid when it breaks.

parts.heading: Three principles, one machine
parts.voice: systems — describes registration as a mechanism with defined outputs before any case law appears
body: Registered conveyancing runs on three design principles, and almost every rule in this lesson is one of them doing its job. First, the mirror principle: the register is meant to reflect the complete state of title, so that anyone can read off who owns what and what burdens sit on it. Second, the curtain principle: certain interests — trusts being the classic example — are kept off the register entirely and dealt with 'behind the curtain', so a buyer doesn't need to investigate them to get good title. Third, the insurance principle: if the register is wrong, the state guarantees it — the person who loses out because of a mistake is compensated, rather than left to unwind the transaction.

Keep these three running in the background as you read the rest of this lesson. Registrable dispositions exist to keep the mirror accurate. The priority rule exists to tell a buyer what they can trust the mirror to show. Alteration and indemnity exist because no mirror is perfect, and the system has to decide who absorbs that cost.

None of this is decoration. Exam questions on this topic are, underneath the facts, always asking the same thing: what does the register say, and what happens when what it says turns out to be incomplete or wrong?

components.label: The three principles of registered title
points: Mirror principle — the register reflects the whole of the title, so it can be read rather than investigated
Curtain principle — some interests (notably trusts) are kept off the register and don't need to concern a buyer
Insurance principle — the state guarantees the accuracy of the register and compensates for loss caused by its mistakes

interaction.prompt: A buyer of registered land is told they don't need to worry about the details of a trust behind the title, provided the purchase money is paid correctly. Which principle explains this?
options: The curtain principle
The mirror principle
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The curtain principle keeps trust arrangements off the register and out of the buyer's concern — that's precisely what overreaching (covered in the next lesson) relies on.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: That's the curtain principle, not the mirror. The mirror principle is about the register showing legal title accurately; the curtain is about what the buyer is entitled to ignore entirely.

parts.heading: What has to go through the machine: registrable dispositions
parts.voice: structural — a reference part built around the statute itself
body: Not every transaction affecting land needs to be registered to take effect at all — but a defined list of dispositions of a registered estate only take effect at law once they are registered. Until registration happens, the disposition takes effect only in equity, if at all. This is the mechanism that keeps the mirror accurate: legal title doesn't quietly shift on a handshake or a signed transfer sitting in a drawer.

Section 27 lists the registrable dispositions — the main ones a student needs cold are a transfer of the registered estate, the grant of a lease of more than seven years, and the grant of a legal charge (mortgage). Section 29 then supplies the priority rule for registered dispositions made for valuable consideration, and section 30 does the same for registered charges.

Section 58 is the quiet workhorse behind all of this: it provides that where a person is registered as proprietor, the legal estate is deemed to vest in them — even if the registration was in fact based on a defective transfer. Registration is what does the work, not the underlying document.

components.text: If a disposition of a registered estate or registered charge is required to be completed by registration, it does not operate at law until the relevant registration requirements are met. The dispositions listed include a transfer, the grant of a lease for a term of more than seven years, and the grant of a legal charge.
elements: A disposition of a registered estate or charge
Falls within the list in s 27(2) (transfer, lease > 7 years, legal charge, etc.)
Does not operate at law until registered

components.text: If, on the entry of a person in the register as proprietor of a legal estate, the legal estate would not otherwise be vested in him, it is deemed to be vested in him as a result of the registration.
elements: Legal estate is deemed vested by that entry alone
Applies even where the underlying disposition was defective

interaction.prompt: A landlord grants a tenant a lease for six years, signed and handed over, but never registers it. Under s 27, what is the legal status of the lease?
options: It cannot operate at law and has no effect of any kind
It takes effect at law immediately — a six-year lease isn't a registrable disposition
It can take effect only in equity, if the requirements for an equitable lease are otherwise met
interaction.explanation: A lease of seven years or less is outside the s 27(2) list of registrable dispositions — it can be a legal lease without registration at all. The six-year term is the detail that changes the answer: it falls below the registration threshold, so s 27 never engages.

parts.heading: The priority rule in action: a registration gap
parts.voice: case-narrative — walks a transaction through time so the priority rule shows its own logic
body: The basic priority rule under s 29 is easy to misstate as 'first in time wins'. It's closer to the opposite. Where a registrable disposition is made for valuable consideration and duly registered, it takes priority over any interest affecting the estate immediately before the disposition — unless that interest was protected by an entry in the register at the time, or falls within the small category of overriding interests that bind regardless (the subject of the next lesson).

Picture the timeline. On Monday, the registered proprietor grants an unprotected equitable interest — say, an estate contract that is never noted. On Wednesday, the same proprietor sells the whole property to a buyer for full value. On Friday, the buyer's transfer is registered. Under s 29, the buyer takes free of the Monday interest, even though it existed first in time, precisely because it wasn't protected by an entry and isn't overriding.

The lesson to take from the timeline isn't 'registration beats everything' — an interest protected by a notice on Monday would have survived the Wednesday sale untouched. The lesson is that the priority rule rewards protection, not existence. An unprotected interest doesn't disappear — the original grantor still owes whatever obligation they created — but it stops binding the land itself once a registered disposition for value goes through the machine.

components.definition: An entry on the register that protects the priority of a third-party interest — it does not guarantee the interest is valid, only that, if valid, it will bind a later registered proprietor.

interaction.prompt: Put these events in the order needed for the s 29 priority rule to defeat the Monday interest.
items: Registered proprietor grants an equitable interest, unprotected by any entry
The same proprietor enters a sale of the whole property for valuable consideration
The buyer's transfer is completed by registration
The buyer takes the estate free of the unprotected interest
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the mechanism. Registration for value is what triggers s 29 — until the buyer is actually registered, the interest is still at risk of being protected, and the outcome isn't fixed.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — nothing is decided until registration of the buyer's own disposition actually happens. Before that point, the unprotected interest could still be protected and change the outcome.

parts.heading: Protecting an interest: entries that survive a sale
parts.voice: practical — written as instructions for how a third party actually protects themselves
body: If priority rewards protection, the obvious question is: how does a third party protect an interest that isn't itself registrable? The main tool is a notice entered against the burdened title — this doesn't create the interest or guarantee it exists, but it puts any future buyer on the register on notice, so that if the underlying interest is valid, s 29 no longer helps the buyer defeat it.

Notice is available for most third-party interests capable of binding successors — estate contracts, restrictive covenants, equitable leases, home rights under the Family Law Act 1996, and more. It is not available for interests under a trust of land: those are the interests the curtain principle deliberately keeps off the register, and they're dealt with instead through overreaching, not notice.

Get this distinction wrong in an exam and you'll spend a paragraph trying to protect a beneficial interest under a trust by 'entering a notice' — which the Land Registration Act 2002 does not permit. The register protects the interests it's designed to show; trusts are designed to stay hidden.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often suggest a beneficiary under a trust of land should simply 'register a notice' to protect their interest against a buyer.
components.whyItsWrong: Interests under a trust of land cannot be protected by notice — the Act specifically excludes them, because the curtain principle is designed to keep trusts off the register altogether. Their protection route is overreaching, not notice; that mechanism is covered in the next lesson.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that tells you a notice cannot be used to protect this interest.
interaction.scenarioText: Priya holds an equitable interest in a registered property under a trust of land, having contributed to the purchase price. Her solicitor asks the Land Registry to enter a notice against the title to protect her interest before the legal owner remortgages.
tappableSpans: equitable interest in a registered property
enter a notice against the title
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. It isn't the fact that Priya's interest is equitable that rules out a notice — plenty of equitable interests are protected that way. It's that this equitable interest arises under a trust of land, which the Act excludes from protection by notice.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the fact that identifies the source of Priya's interest, not just that it's equitable. The problem isn't that her interest is equitable — it's what kind of equitable interest it is.

parts.heading: When the machine gets it wrong: alteration and indemnity
parts.voice: case-narrative — builds the doctrine around Swift 1st as a worked problem
body: Sometimes the register is simply wrong — a forged transfer gets registered, or an interest that should have been removed remains. Schedule 4 gives the court and the registrar power to alter the register to correct a mistake. Where that alteration prejudicially affects the title of a registered proprietor in possession, the more specific term used is rectification, and it can only happen in limited circumstances — broadly, where the proprietor caused or contributed to the mistake, or where it would for some other reason be unjust not to rectify.

Schedule 8 is the insurance side of the machine: a person who suffers loss because of rectification, or because a mistake in the register is corrected against them, or because the registrar refuses to correct an obvious mistake, can claim an indemnity from the state. The two schedules work as a pair — Schedule 4 decides whether the register gets fixed, Schedule 8 decides who is compensated for the fallout.

Swift 1st v Chief Land Registrar is the case that tests whether students actually understand this pairing. A fraudulent transfer led to the registration of a charge in favour of Swift 1st. The Court of Appeal had to work out whether removing the fraudulently registered charge was an 'alteration' that also counted as a 'rectification' for indemnity purposes — because whether Swift 1st could claim compensation turned on that classification, not on whether the register had simply been corrected.

components.caseName: Swift 1st Ltd v Chief Land Registrar
components.factsShort: A fraudster used a forged transfer to become registered proprietor and then charged the property to Swift 1st. When the fraud came to light, the registrar removed the charge from the register.
components.ratioShort: Correcting the register to remove an entry made under a mistake (including one caused by fraud) is an alteration; whether it also amounts to a rectification — engaging the indemnity provisions — depends on whether it prejudicially affects the title of a registered proprietor in possession.

expanded.facts: A fraudster forged documents to become the registered proprietor of a property, then used that registration to grant a legal charge to Swift 1st Ltd, a commercial lender, in return for a loan that was never repaid. When the true owner discovered the fraud, the registrar altered the register to remove both the fraudulent transfer and the charge. Swift 1st, left with a worthless charge, sought an indemnity.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that removing the fraudulently obtained charge from the register was properly classified as an alteration to correct a mistake. Whether Swift 1st could recover an indemnity depended on characterising that alteration correctly under Schedule 8 — the court examined closely whether Swift 1st, as the registered chargee, had ever truly held a valid registered interest capable of being 'rectified' away, or whether the charge had been a mistake in the register from the moment it was entered.
expanded.significance: The case is the standard illustration that alteration and rectification are not simply interchangeable words for 'correcting the register' — the label given to the correction determines who, if anyone, is entitled to an indemnity under Schedule 8, which makes the classification exercise the whole ballgame for a claimant like Swift 1st.

interaction.prompt: A forged transfer results in a stranger becoming registered proprietor of Leon's house while Leon is abroad. On his return, Leon successfully has the register corrected to restore his name. He is out of pocket from legal costs incurred sorting out the fraud. What does Schedule 8 potentially offer him?
options: Nothing — Schedule 8 only covers registered proprietors who keep their registration
A possible indemnity for loss suffered because of the mistake and its correction, subject to the Schedule 8 conditions
Automatic compensation equal to the full market value of the property, regardless of his actual loss
interaction.explanation: Schedule 8 indemnifies loss caused by a mistake in the register and by its correction, not just loss from a correction that goes against you — but it is not an automatic, uncapped payout: the loss has to be shown, and the Schedule's specific conditions and exclusions still apply.

testPool.prompt: Name the three design principles said to underpin the system of registered title.
acceptableAnswers: mirror principle, curtain principle, insurance principle
testPool.modelAnswer: The mirror principle, the curtain principle, and the insurance principle.

testPool.prompt: Under s 58 LRA 2002, what is the effect of a person being entered on the register as proprietor, even where the underlying transfer to them was defective?
options: The legal estate is deemed vested in them by the registration itself
The registration is automatically void and must be reversed

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT listed among the registrable dispositions in s 27 LRA 2002?
options: A transfer of the registered estate
The grant of a legal charge
The grant of a lease for a term of more than seven years
The grant of a licence to occupy for six months
testPool.trapExplanation: A licence to occupy creates no proprietary interest at all, so it was never a candidate for registration in the first place — it isn't excluded from s 27 for being too short, the way a short lease is, but because it isn't the right kind of right.

testPool.prompt: Under s 29 LRA 2002, a registered disposition for valuable consideration takes priority over a pre-existing interest UNLESS that interest is protected by an entry in the register, or falls into which other category?
options: It is an overriding interest
It was created more than five years before the disposition
The original grantor has since died

testPool.prompt: Order the events so that a buyer takes free of a competing equitable interest under s 29.
items: An unprotected equitable interest is created over the land
The registered proprietor disposes of the land for valuable consideration
No notice is entered to protect the equitable interest before completion
The buyer's disposition is completed by registration

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, highlight the sentence that states the operative rule on priority.
testPool.passage: A registered disposition made for valuable consideration takes priority over any interest affecting the estate immediately before the disposition. This is subject to two exceptions: interests protected by an entry in the register at the time of the disposition, and interests that override the disposition regardless of protection. An unprotected interest that falls outside both exceptions loses priority once the disposition is registered.
testPool.ratioSentence: A registered disposition made for valuable consideration takes priority over any interest affecting the estate immediately before the disposition.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a beneficial interest under a trust of land can be protected by entering a notice against the title?
sliderLabels: Definitely can be protected by notice
Definitely cannot be protected by notice
testPool.explanation: Interests under a trust of land are specifically excluded from protection by notice under the LRA 2002 — the curtain principle keeps them off the register, and overreaching, not notice, is their protection route.

testPool.prompt: Anna grants her neighbour a right of way by deed over her registered land. The neighbour never registers a notice. Anna later sells the land for full value to a buyer who has never heard of the right of way, and the sale is duly registered. Can the buyer be bound by the right of way?
options: No — an unprotected easement of this kind cannot bind a registered disposition for value under s 29
Yes — an easement created by deed always binds regardless of registration
Yes — because the neighbour used the right of way before the sale
testPool.explanation: Unless the easement is protected by notice, or qualifies as overriding, s 29 lets the buyer take free of it despite the deed. Whether it could instead qualify as overriding is a question for the next lesson on Schedule 3.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that decides whether a notice was available to protect this interest.
testPool.scenarioText: Marcus enters into a contract to buy a flat off-plan from a developer. Before completion, the developer sells the whole site to a third party. Marcus's solicitor had entered a notice against the developer's title as soon as the contract was signed.
tappableSpans: contract to buy a flat off-plan
entered a notice against the developer's title
as soon as the contract was signed
testPool.correctSpan: entered a notice against the developer's title
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. An estate contract is exactly the kind of interest a notice is designed to protect — because it was entered before the sale, Marcus's contractual interest survives the developer's later disposition.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: The outcome here turns on the protective step that was actually taken, not on the nature of the contract itself. Look for the fact describing what Marcus's solicitor did.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is more likely to result in rectification (rather than a non-prejudicial alteration) under Schedule 4?
testPool.scenarioA: The register is corrected to remove a spent restrictive covenant that no longer affects anyone's title or possession.
testPool.scenarioB: The register is corrected to remove a registered proprietor who was in possession, after it emerges their registration was based on a forged transfer.
testPool.explanation: B affects the title of a registered proprietor in possession — that is what elevates a correction from a routine alteration to rectification, and triggers both the stricter Schedule 4 conditions and the possibility of an indemnity claim under Schedule 8.

testPool.prompt: Following Swift 1st, a lender's charge is removed from the register after it turns out to have been granted by a fraudster who was never the true owner. The lender claims an indemnity under Schedule 8. What is the key question the court must resolve first?
options: Whether the removal of the charge is properly characterised as a rectification affecting a registered proprietor, engaging Schedule 8
Whether the lender acted in good faith when granting the loan
Whether the fraudster has since been convicted of a criminal offence
testPool.explanation: Swift 1st turns on classification: an indemnity claim under Schedule 8 depends on the correction being characterised as a rectification of the kind the Schedule covers, not merely on whether the lender behaved reasonably.

testPool.prompt: Dana enters into a written contract to buy a registered freehold from Oliver, paying a deposit. Before completion, Oliver secretly grants a legal charge over the property to a bank in exchange for a loan, and the bank registers the charge. Dana had not entered a notice to protect her contract. Analyse whether the bank's charge takes priority over Dana's contractual interest.
factsToOrder: Dana has a contract to buy, but it is only an equitable interest until completion
Dana did not protect her interest by entering a notice
The bank's charge is a registrable disposition made for valuable consideration
The bank's charge is duly registered
No exception under s 29 (protection by notice, or overriding status) applies on these facts

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the bank's registered charge takes priority over Dana's unprotected contractual interest.
modelAnswer.rule: Under s 29 LRA 2002, a registered disposition made for valuable consideration takes priority over a pre-existing interest unless that interest is protected by an entry in the register or is overriding.
modelAnswer.application: Dana's contract creates only an equitable interest, which needed to be protected by notice to bind a later disposition; she never entered one. The bank's charge is a registrable disposition (s 27) made for value and has been duly registered. There is nothing on the facts suggesting Dana's interest could be overriding, since it is not linked to her being in actual occupation.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The bank's charge takes priority over Dana's contractual interest, which — though it survives as a personal claim against Oliver — no longer binds the land.

testPool.prompt: Which statement best captures why a notice on the register is described as protecting 'priority' rather than 'validity'?
options: Because a notice guarantees the underlying interest exists and is enforceable
Because a notice only determines whether an interest, if valid, will bind a later registered disposition — it does not itself create or validate the interest
Because notices can only be entered by the Land Registry, never by the interest-holder
testPool.trapExplanation: It's tempting to treat a notice as a stamp of approval on the interest itself. It isn't — the Registry does not adjudicate whether the underlying right actually exists when it enters a notice; that question is left open for the courts if it's ever disputed.

testPool.prompt: A restrictive covenant is properly protected by a notice on the burdened title before a sale. The land is later sold to a new registered proprietor. Is the new proprietor bound by the covenant?
options: Yes — the notice preserved the covenant's priority against a later registered disposition
No — restrictive covenants can never bind a buyer under the LRA 2002

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson is treating registration as a race that unprotected interests can still somehow win by being 'first'. They can't. Section 29 rewards protection, not chronology — check what was entered on the register, not what happened first in time.
